A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FineXtract research under different titles. All 17 pages of v1 and 18 pages of v2, including their appendices, are readable. Equations, tables, and figures can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original extraction experiments on WikiArt, DreamBooth, and real-world checkpoints, alongside ablations, defense evaluations, caption extraction, and computational measurements.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds experiments involving recovered captions, mixed datasets, FLUX, guidance components, defense quality, and longer training captions.

M1.justification: The guidance procedure in Equations 3–13, SSCD-based clique clustering in Section 4.3, and Appendix A caption-extraction algorithm remain unchanged. The added experiments evaluate the existing method and its components without establishing a revised extraction procedure.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained individual-artist and object datasets, v2 evaluates combined DreamBooth/WikiArt classes and mixtures of multiple artists. It also tests image extraction using recovered captions and caption extraction after substantial prompt expansion (Appendices A.5, F, and J). These additions substantially broaden training-distribution and caption-condition coverage.

E2.justification: v1 Figure 4 evaluates FineXtract alone across training-image and generation counts; v2 adds CFG to both corresponding comparisons. Direct Text2img+Clustering and CFG+Clustering remain the comparators in the retained benchmark tables.

E3.justification: The original benchmark settings remain unchanged, but v2 introduces several additional evaluation designs: mixed classes containing five DreamBooth and five WikiArt images, mixtures of 1/2/5 artists, FLUX.1 [dev] LoRA training for 150 iterations, and a k=0 guidance-component comparison. DINO and CLIP-IQA are added to evaluate fidelity and image quality in mixture and defense experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds a model-guidance-only ablation, comparisons using full/recovered/empty captions, sensitivity analyses for dataset heterogeneity and prompt length, and quantitative assessments of defense-induced quality changes. These extend substantially beyond v1's existing guidance-scale, correction-term, generation-count, and defense-effectiveness analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions present point estimates and qualitative examples without reporting repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The additional results do not introduce uncertainty-estimation practices.

E6.justification: The original benchmark and computational-cost values are retained, while v2 adds substantial results in Tables 7 and 9–13, Figure 10, and the CFG curves in Figure 4. Table 7 reports FineXtract A-ESR0.6 of 0.15 with recovered captions versus 0.35 with full captions and 0.00 with empty captions. New FLUX results in Table 11 favor CFG on AS and A-ESR0.6, while FineXtract slightly leads on A-ESR0.7; these are additional results, not same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: The distribution-interpolation assumptions, score derivations in Equations 3–13, and caption-inversion mathematics in Equations 14–20 are retained. There is no substantive new mathematical definition, assumption, proof, or derivation.

C1.justification: Both versions retain the same extraction objective, distribution-extrapolation and clustering contributions, approximately 20% extraction claim, and privacy/copyright motivation. The revised title and abstract wording do not materially redefine these central claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations linking heterogeneous data to poorer model learning, attributing most extraction benefit to model guidance, explaining persistence of defense transformations, and identifying difficulties with longer captions. Some new interpretations conflict with the evidence: Appendix H claims consistent FLUX improvement despite Table 11, and Appendix F.2 claims declining extraction success although Table 10 gives FineXtract A-ESR0.6 values of 0.22, 0.20, and 0.23.

D1.justification: v2 adds a FineXtract code-availability link, describes the FLUX setup using Diffusers defaults and 150 training iterations, and documents GPT-4-based prompt expansion. The original SD fine-tuning hyperparameters and A100 computational measurements remain unchanged; the computational-cost disclosure moves into Section 5.1.

R1.justification: v2 adds Ren et al. (2024), Wen et al. (2024b), and Wang et al. (2023). Section 2.2 adds an argument that inference-time memorization defenses are insufficient with accessible weights and that data-selection defenses are poorly suited to few-shot personalization. The original research positioning otherwise remains intact.

P1.justification: Most shared prose and the main section sequence are retained. v2 changes the title and author information, lightly edits the abstract, moves computational-cost discussion into Section 5.1, reorganizes appendix labels, and adds acknowledgments and an impact statement. Extensive rewriting of the existing scientific narrative is not evident.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the single-column main text with a two-column conference layout, substantially resizing and repositioning existing figures and tables. It moves the computational-cost table into the main text, changes Figure 4's curves, legends, and vertical ranges, and adds several experimental tables and the Figure 10 guidance ablation.

improvement.justification: v2 usefully connects caption recovery to image extraction in Table 7, expands robustness and mechanism evidence, and reports code access. However, new generalization claims conflict with Tables 10 and 11. Moreover, Table 11's FLUX metric triplets exactly match unrelated rows in Table 12 without explanation. The PDFs do not resolve whether the new numerical reporting or accompanying interpretations require correction. These reliability problems coexist with useful additions, preventing a reliable judgment of net overall quality improvement.
